To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the crustal and upper-mantle structure of the Nova Scotia margin is dominated by Mesozoic extension that was controlled by preexisting fabric in the crust and that the crustal thickness of the continental shelf and upper continental slope is about 25 km.

(1) the crust below the continental slope is thinned to 10 km and is underlain by a high-velocity (6.9 km/s) lower crust; (2) the ocean–continent transition is marked by a zone of crustal thinning, a Moho uplift of ∼2 km, and a zone of high velocity (8.2 km/s) mantle; (3) the Moho is not continuous and is disrupted by normal faults;

(1) the crustal thickness decreases toward the continental margin; (2) there is no evidence of magmatic underplating of the continental crust, and (3) the crust is thinned by faulting in the lower crust and by magmatic intrusion in the upper mantle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the continental crust and the lithosphere.
the structure of the crust and upper mantle in the vicinity of the continental margin off eastern Canada.
the structure of the crust and upper mantle beneath the Nova Scotia continental shelf and slope and the nature of the ocean–continent transition.
